title: How Our Attraction to Natural Fixes Can Stymie Climate Progress
gist: A University of Colorado Boulder-led study surveyed 1,000 Americans on 10 climate-change solutions (carbon capture, tree planting, nuclear, wind, solar, etc.) to test how perceiving a fix as 'unnatural' affects public support for tax-funded climate programs.

themes.theme: The 'appeal to nature' bias applied to climate policy

insights.claim: Humans have an innate preference for things perceived as 'natural,' assuming that what comes from nature is better, healthier, and more moral — a cognitive tendency known as the 'appeal to nature' fallacy.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: This well-documented cognitive bias can be applied predictively to climate policy: solutions framed as 'unnatural' (e.g., nuclear power, engineered carbon capture) may face public resistance regardless of their actual efficacy.
insights.quote: Former debate club kids will recognize this rhetorical trick as the “appeal to nature” fallacy, but there’s a good reason it gets bandied about—it works

insights.claim: A new study published in the journal Communications Earth & Environment, led by researchers from the University of Colorado Boulder, surveyed 1,000 Americans about their views on 10 different methods for tackling climate change, including carbon-removal countermeasures like carbon capture and tree planting, and green-energy solutions like nuclear, wind, and solar power.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Quantifies public opinion research design that will inform which climate technologies can win broad taxpayer-funded political support versus which face a 'unnaturalness' penalty.
insights.quote: A team of psychologists and environmental scientists led by researchers from the University of Colorado Boulder surveyed 1,000 Americans about their views on 10 different methods for tackling climate change.
insights.locator: As our many inborn biases go

insights.claim: Survey respondents were asked whether they'd support a broad-based, tax-funded program to implement each climate-change fix, and separately rated each solution on how natural, beneficial, risky, familiar, or frightening they perceived it to be.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Multi-dimensional framing (naturalness, risk, familiarity, fear) lets researchers isolate which perceptual factor most drives public willingness to fund a given climate technology, useful for messaging and policy design around energy transition technologies.
insights.quote: Respondents were specifically asked if they’d support a broad-based program to implement the climate-change fixes with their tax dollars, as well as how natural, beneficial, risky, familiar, or frightening they deemed the solutions.
insights.locator: A team of psychologists and environmental scientists
